questions.question: Distinguish the cash budget from the projected statement of comprehensive income, naming items that appear in only one of the two.
questions.expected_answer: The projected income statement forecasts PROFIT on the accrual basis: income earned against expenses incurred, so a credit sale belongs to the month the goods change hands, and depreciation and bad debts appear because value is consumed and losses are expected. The cash budget forecasts the BANK BALANCE on the cash basis: a credit sale enters only when the debtor actually pays, depreciation never appears because no money moves, and bad debts are simply receipts that fail to arrive. Unique to the cash budget: capital contributed, drawings, loans raised and capital instalments repaid, assets bought for cash, and VAT paid over. Unique to the projected income statement: depreciation, bad debts and the accrued portions of expenses. The sorting question for every line: does it move money this month, earn income or consume value this month, or both?

questions.question: Build June's collection from debtors given: sales 30% cash and 70% credit; debtors pay 60% in the following month less a 5% discount, 25% in the second month, 10% in the third, and 5% is written off. Credit sales were R112 000 (March), R126 000 (April) and R168 000 (May), with June sales of R280 000.
questions.expected_answer: From May: 60% of R168 000 = R100 800, less the 5% settlement discount = R95 760. From April: 25% of R126 000 = R31 500. From March: 10% of R112 000 = R11 200. Total collection from debtors in June = R138 460. Adding June's cash sales of 30% x R280 000 = R84 000 gives R222 460 of receipts from trading. Three disciplines: the discount is deducted only from the prompt 60% portion that earns it; each month's collections draw on three earlier months' sales, so the schedule is laid out as a grid; and the 5% written off never enters the cash budget — it appears in the projected income statement as bad debts.

questions.question: Explain how a business can forecast a strong profit and a dangerous cash shortfall in the same month, and describe how variance analysis should be read afterwards.
questions.expected_answer: Timing. Credit sales made in June earn June's profit but arrive as cash in July, August and September; the stock behind them was paid for in May; wages go out in June; and an asset may be bought for cash in June. The income statement says the business is thriving while the bank cannot cover month-end salaries — both are true, and a complete answer names the specific items rather than saying 'one is cash and one is profit'. Afterwards, variance analysis compares budget to actual line by line, stating both figures, the rand and percentage difference, and favourable or unfavourable, then interpreting: sales below budget may mean fading demand, a competitor, or an over-hopeful forecast; an expense under budget is not automatically good, since advertising at half the plan may explain the sales shortfall beside it. Variances are read as a set, and the monthly comparison is what makes the budget a control rather than a wish.
